name: Yowlah

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: An experienced Yowlah practitioner or heritage educator.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Yowlah originated as a Bedouin war dance performed after victory in tribal battles or successful pearl diving.
It is a ritual of tribal unity and defense, now serving as a symbol of national heritage in the UAE and Oman.
on_screen: Map: United Arab Emirates, Oman · Middle East
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed for weddings, national celebrations, state visits, and football matches.
It signifies tribal unity, defense, solidarity, and victory.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Performers form two rows facing each other.
Men hop from foot to foot while holding bamboo sticks, swords, or dummy rifles.
They move their heads and sticks in synchronization with the rhythm.
Watch for Naash.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (OjPQhSzFD5A)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Two rows of men facing each other; women stand at the front.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music features large and small drums, tambourines, brass cymbals, leather bagpipes, and flutes.
The melody consists of seven tones in an irregular repeated pattern, accompanied by chanted poetry.
Listen for the large drums, small drums, tambourines, brass cymbals.
A rhythmic, percussive soundscape driven by drums and cymbals, layered with melodic flute or bagpipe lines and vocal chanting.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Men typically wear the white dishdasha.
Women wear traditional dresses.
The dance is performed in open spaces during weddings, festivals, and official ceremonies.
on_screen: Image gallery: 3 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: The lead performer is usually an inherited role responsible for training others.
Variations include the Razfah, Ardah, al-harbiyya, and al-wahabbiyya, the latter of which is found in rural and coastal areas of Ras Al Khayma and Fujairah.
Rooted in Bedouin martial traditions and tribal war rituals.
